newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Rwanda genocide horror played out in U.N. court.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda genocide horror played out in U.N. court.

text.p: A 70-year-old Rwandan woman took five minutes at the U.N. genocide trials last week to locate in court the man she said beat and tortured her. Then she bowed and shook him warmly by the hand.

Judges, lawyers and spectators were stunned by a gesture so at odds with the Hutu woman's testimony. Was it an act of forgiveness, or deference to her former commune leader? Or was it a simple reflex?

Rwandan's thought it was traditional subservience to those in authority. It had no effect on Jean-Paul Akayesu, 43, who has pleaded not guilty to charges of genocide and crimes against humanity. He remained impassive.
Akayesu, the former mayor of central Taba commune, is the first to be tried by the U.N. court set up in November 1994. If convicted he faces life imprisonment, the court's highest penalty.
Some of the horror of Rwanda's genocide is being turned into courtroom drama in the long, stuffy room on the fourth floor of Arusha's run-down conference centre.
The panel of three judges sit on a wooden dais facing the witness box with the accused behind a glass screen to the right.
Spectators and the media are separated from the proceedings by a bullet-proof glass screen that divides the chamber in two and headphones carry French and English translations.

Under a ruling by the judges, Akayesu was permitted to act as his own defence counsel and cross-examine the first three Rwandan witnesses personally. So in a series of confrontations accused met victims face-to-face.
Akayesu towered over the second witness, a Hutu coffee farmer known only as "C" to protect his identity, to inspect scars on his back and face -- wounds the witness said Akayesu inflicted.
He tried to undermine the credibility of witness "K", a Tutsi genocide survivor who said she watched him order eight Tutsis hacked to death outside his office.

And he clashed with the 70-year-old Hutu woman who in testimony to the prosecution said Akayesu beat her, bound her hand and foot and threatened to run her over because she refused to say where a Tutsi woman named Alexia was hiding.
"Did you not want to crush me with that car? You told me to lie down on the ground and you were going to drive over me to crush me," the woman screamed in answer to a question from Akayesu.

Judges say they hope the start of trials will shift the spotlight from the tribunal's internal problems. New U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan vowed "decisive action" to clean up the tribunal after a draft report alleged financial malpractice, mismanagement, nepotism and racism.
"I am much more encouraged than I was two weeks ago now that the trials have started," Swedish judge Lennart Aspegren told reporters.
A total of 11 people have so far been indicted by the tribunal, but a verdict in Akayesu's case is not expected for several months.

The confrontation between Akayesu and the old woman who walked into court limping and supported by a stick replayed just one episode of the Taba commune massacres -- itself a fraction of the genocide in which an estimated 800,000 were killed.
Many more gruesome episodes could be played out before the court in the coming months.
